slides.title: 1.1 · Can change occur at an instant?
slides.html:
Novel Prep · AP Calculus AB / BC

Unit 1 · Section 1.1

Can change occur at an instant?

Jump to a section or press Next to begin.

slides.title: Why we need calculus
slides.html:
Launch

Motion at an instant

Motion at an instant

LaunchA speedometer moment

Average speed is easy; instantaneous speed is not.

Big Idea

A car travels 60 miles in 2 hours — average speed is 30 mph. But what does the speedometer read at exactly 1:00 PM?

That is not an average over time. It is a rate at an instant.

What it means

Instantaneous rate asks how fast something changes at one input value.

Why it matters

This question leads to derivatives and the limit idea.

How to recognize

Words like “at t = 2 exactly” or “at this moment.”

Common mistake

Using a long interval and calling it instantaneous.

How to check

Shrink the interval and see if the average rates stabilize.

slides.title: Position graph s(t) = t² + 1
slides.html:
Visual Investigation

Position vs time

Position vs time

VisualRead the curve

Slope of a secant = average rate on that time interval.

slides.title: Average rate of change
slides.html:
Concept & Definition

Average rate of change

Average rate of change

Definition · Average rate of change on [a, b]
\[\displaystyle \text{Average rate}=\frac{s(b)-s(a)}{b-a}\]

Geometrically: slope of the secant line connecting the two points on the graph.

Units: (output units) per (input unit) — here, meters per second.

Key Point · At t = 2
\[\displaystyle \frac{s(3)-s(2)}{3-2}=\frac{10-5}{1}=5\ \text{m/s}\]

This is the average velocity from t = 2 s to t = 3 s — not the velocity at t = 2.

slides.html:
Visual Investigation

Table of average rates

Table of average rates

VisualLet h → 0

Use both positive and negative h to approach t = 2.

AP Checkpoint
From both sides, average rates approach 4. That limiting value is the instantaneous rate at \(t=2\).

slides.html:

slides.title: The difference quotient
slides.html:
Concept & Definition

Difference quotient

Difference quotient

Definition · Difference quotient at t = a
\[\displaystyle \frac{s(a+h)-s(a)}{h}\]
  • s(a+h) − s(a) — vertical rise Δs on the graph
  • h — horizontal run (time interval)
  • Quotient — secant slope = rise ÷ run
Key Point · Preview only
We will formalize approach in Section 1.2. Here: shorter intervals \(\Rightarrow\) secant slope \(\Rightarrow\) instantaneous rate.

slides.title: Why shrinking the interval works
slides.html:
Why It Works

From average to instantaneous

From average to instantaneous

ReasonSame idea on both sides

Average rates stabilize when the interval is tiny.

Big Idea

When \(h\) is small, the secant slope \(\dfrac{s(a+h)-s(a)}{h}\) measures change over a short interval — closer to what happens at \(t=a\).

If left-side (\(h<0\)) and right-side (\(h>0\)) averages approach the same number, that common value is the instantaneous rate.

AP Checkpoint
We are not claiming \(h=0\). We observe a pattern as \(h\to 0\).

slides.title: Worked example: simplify the difference quotient
slides.html:
Definition · Problem

Find the instantaneous rate at t = 2 by simplifying the difference quotient.

Key Point · Representation

Algebra + table + secant graph all describe the same limiting slope.

Walk through the solution

Step 1. Build: \(\dfrac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}=\dfrac{(2+h)^2+1-5}{h}\).

Step 2. Expand: \((2+h)^2+1-5 = 4+4h+h^2\).

Step 3. Simplify: \(\dfrac{4h+h^2}{h}=4+h\) for \(h\neq 0\).

Step 4. Interpret: as \(h\to 0\), the rate approaches \(4\) m/s.

AP Checkpoint
Conclusion: The instantaneous rate of change of s at t = 2 is 4 m/s.
Key Point · Check

Secant slope on [2, 2.01] ≈ 4.01; tangent slope matches 4.

slides.title: Error analysis: plugging in h = 0
slides.html:
Contrast / Error Analysis

Why h = 0 is not allowed yet

Why h = 0 is not allowed yet

Common Mistake

Substituting \(h=0\) gives \(\dfrac{s(2)-s(2)}{0}=\dfrac{0}{0}\), which is undefined.

Why wrong: \(h=0\) means “no interval,” so the difference quotient does not describe a secant slope.

Correct move: simplify algebraically first, then let \(h\to 0\).

slides.title: Practice: compute an average rate
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Use (change in output) / (change in input) on [1, 4].

For \(s(t)=t^2+1\), what is the average rate of change on \([1,4]\)?

Choose your answer

\(s(4)=17\), \(s(1)=2\), so average rate \(=\dfrac{17-2}{4-1}=5\). B uses wrong denominator. C omits division by time. D reverses the interval sign. A is correct.

slides.title: Practice: interpret a difference quotient
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Interval in denominator → average, not instantaneous.

Buffalo population \(b(t)\), \(t\) years since 1800. What does \(\dfrac{b(50)-b(0)}{50}\) represent?

Choose your answer

A confuses a rate with a population value. C needs a limit of a difference quotient. D misreads “average over 50 years.” B is correct: average rate on [0, 50].

slides.title: Practice: instantaneous rate setup
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Instantaneous requires a limiting process, not one finite interval.

Which expression represents the instantaneous rate of \(s(t)=t^2+1\) at \(t=2\)?

Choose your answer

A, D are average rates on one interval. C is position, not rate. B is the definition of instantaneous rate.

slides.title: Exit ticket · 1.1
slides.html:
Exit TicketCheck your learning

Answer each item before revealing.

  1. 1
    State the average rate of \(s(t)=t^2+1\) on \([2,3]\) and interpret it.

    \(\dfrac{s(3)-s(2)}{1}=5\) m/s — average velocity from t=2 to t=3.

  2. 2
    Simplify \(\dfrac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}\) and state the instantaneous rate at \(t=2\).

    Simplifies to \(4+h\); instantaneous rate is 4 m/s.

  3. 3
    Why can't we substitute \(h=0\) into the difference quotient before simplifying?

    It gives \(0/0\) — undefined. We need \(h\neq 0\) for a secant slope.

slides.title: 1.2 · Defining limits and notation
slides.html:
Novel Prep · AP Calculus AB / BC

Unit 1 · Section 1.2

Defining limits and limit notation

Jump to a section or press Next to begin.

slides.title: Limits describe approach, not always value
slides.html:
Launch

Near vs at a point

Near vs at a point

LaunchThe language of approach

We care what happens as x gets close to c.

Big Idea

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L\) describes behavior near \(x=c\), not necessarily at \(x=c\).

What it means

As x approaches c, outputs f(x) approach L.

Why it matters

Limits let us define instantaneous rate and continuity.

How to recognize

Phrase “as x approaches c” or the notation \(x \to c\).

Common mistake

Assuming f(c) must equal L.

How to check

Compare table values near c from both sides.

slides.title: Reading limit notation
slides.html:
Concept & Definition

Symbol by symbol

Symbol by symbol

Definition · Informal limit
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L\]
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x) = 5\]
SymbolMeaning
xinput variable
cthe value x approaches
\(x \to c\)x gets arbitrarily close to c (not necessarily equal)
f(x)output values of the function
Lthe value f(x) approaches
Key Point · Say it aloud

“The limit of f(x) as x approaches c is L.”

slides.html:

slides.title: Representation transfer: graph, table, words
slides.html:
Representation Transfer

One idea — four forms

One idea — four forms

TransferConnect representations

AP questions mix all four.

FormStatement for \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\)
Symbolic\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\)
VerbalAs x approaches 3, f(x) approaches 5.
Table\(x\): 2.9, 2.99, 3.01 \(\Rightarrow f(x)\to 5\)
GraphBranches near x=3 approach height y=5
AP Checkpoint
None of these automatically imply \(f(3)=5\).

slides.title: Worked example: limit vs f(c)
slides.html:
Definition · Problem

Find \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\) and compare to \(f(3)\) for the piecewise function below.

\[f(x)=\begin{cases} x+2 & \text{if } x\neq 3 \\ 10 & \text{if } x=3\end{cases}\]
Key Point · Representation

Algebraic rule for x ≠ 3; separate rule at x = 3.

Walk through the solution

Step 1. For x ≠ 3, f(x) = x + 2, so near 3 the outputs behave like x + 2.

Step 2. Compute: \(\lim_{x\to 3}(x+2)=5\).

Step 3. By definition, \(f(3)=10\).

Step 4. Conclusion: limit exists and equals 5, but \(f(3)\neq 5\).

AP Checkpoint
Conclusion: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\) while \(f(3)=10\).
Key Point · Check

Graph would show open circle at (3,5) and filled dot at (3,10).

Approach (limit)
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x) = 5\]
At the point (value)
\[\displaystyle f(3) = 10\]

slides.title: Contrast: common mis-readings
slides.html:
Contrast / Error Analysis

What the limit does NOT say

What the limit does NOT say

Common Mistake

Wrong: “\(f(3)=5\) because the limit is 5.”

Why: Limits describe approach; \(f(3)\) is read from the definition or filled dot.

Common Mistake

Wrong: “As x approaches 5, f(x) approaches 3” for \(\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)=5\).

Why: The input approaches c and outputs approach L — do not swap numbers.

slides.html:

slides.title: Practice: table to limit statement
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Table values near x=2 approach 5 from both sides.

A table shows \(f(x)\) near \(x=2\): 1.9→4.8, 1.99→4.98, 2.01→5.02, 2.1→5.2. Which limit statement is best supported?

Choose your answer

A matches the table trend. B swaps 2 and 5. C confuses limit with value. D contradicts agreeing sides.

slides.title: Practice: words to symbols
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Input approaches c; outputs approach L.

Which expression matches: “As \(x\) approaches \(-2\), \(f(x)\) approaches \(7\)”?

Choose your answer

A is correct notation. B swaps input and output targets. C is a function value, not a limit. D uses the wrong limit value.

slides.title: Practice: best interpretation
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Match input approach with output approach.

Best interpretation of \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 4} f(x)=8\)?

Choose your answer

A confuses limit with value. B,D swap 4 and 8. C is correct.

slides.title: Practice: limit vs value from graph
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Both statements can be true simultaneously.

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x)=3\) but \(f(2)=1.5\). Which is true?

Choose your answer

Limit 3 and value 1.5 can coexist (Case B). C is correct.

slides.title: Practice: identify the error
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Counterexample: piecewise with f(1) defined differently.

A student says: “Because \(\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)=4\), we know \(f(1)=4\) in all cases.” True?

Choose your answer

B is correct. Case B shows limit 5 with f(3)=10. Limits do not force f(c)=L.

slides.title: Extension: ε–δ definition
slides.html:
Definition · Formal precision (extension)
\[\forall\varepsilon>0,\ \exists\delta>0:\ 0<|x-c|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\]

This formalizes “arbitrarily close.” Not required for AP computation at this stage.

slides.title: Exit ticket · 1.2
slides.html:
Exit TicketCheck your learning

Answer each item before revealing.

  1. 1
    Write \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 5} f(x)=-2\) in words.

    As x approaches 5, f(x) approaches −2.

  2. 2
    True or false: \(f(1)=\lim_{x\to 1} f(x)\) in all cases.

    False. Counterexample: removable hole or jump.

  3. 3
    Name two things that can differ when \(\lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L\).

    \(f(c)\) may be undefined or may equal a value different from L.

slides.title: 1.3 · Limits from graphs
slides.html:
Novel Prep · AP Calculus AB / BC

Unit 1 · Section 1.3

Estimating limits from graphs

Jump to a section or press Next to begin.

slides.title: The four-step graph procedure
slides.html:
Launch

Left → Right → Compare → Value

Left → Right → Compare → Value

LaunchA stable routine

Use the same steps on every graph problem.

Big Idea
  1. Trace from the left — approach \(x=c\) with \(x \lt c\)
  2. Trace from the right — approach \(x=c\) with \(x \gt c\)
  3. Compare — if both branch heights match, the two-sided limit exists
  4. Inspect the filled point — read \(f(c)\) only after you know the limit
What it means

Estimate limits by approaching c on each side of the graph.

Why it matters

Graphs appear on every AP exam before algebraic limit rules.

How to recognize

Open circle vs filled dot; left vs right branch heights.

Common mistake

Reading the filled dot before comparing sides.

How to check

Re-trace both branches; label \(L^{-}\) and \(L^{+}\) before deciding.

slides.title: One-sided limits
slides.html:
Concept & Definition

One-sided limits

One-sided limits

Definition · Left-hand and right-hand limits

Each one-sided limit describes one direction of approach to \(x=c\).

Left-hand limit
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) = L\]
Right-hand limit
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) = M\]
Key Point · Read the superscript

Minus (−) means \(x\) approaches \(c\) from the left (\(x \lt c\)). Plus (+) means \(x\) approaches from the right (\(x \gt c\)). The superscript is not part of the number \(c\).

ExampleJump at x = 3

Different branch heights on each side.

From the left
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x) = -1\]
From the right
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x) = 4\]
Two-sided limit
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\ \text{does not exist}\]

The left approach gives -1 but the right gives 4. Because \(L^{-} \neq L^{+}\), the two-sided limit at x = 3 does not exist.

slides.title: Two-sided limit exists when sides agree
slides.html:
Why It Works

Combining one-sided limits

Combining one-sided limits

Definition · Two-sided limit

The two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.

\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) = L\]
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) = L\]
\[\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\qquad \lim_{x\to c} f(x)=L\]

If \(L^{-}\neq L^{+}\), the two-sided limit does not exist — even if \(f(c)\) is defined.

Approach (limit)
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) = 3\]
At the point (value)
\[\displaystyle f(2) = 1.5\]
Key Point · Limit vs value

Branches approach height 3 at \(x=2\), but the filled dot is at 1.5. The limit exists; the function is not continuous there.

slides.title: Worked example: piecewise at x = 2
slides.html:
Definition · Problem

Use the four-step procedure on the piecewise graph at \(x=2\).

Show worked model
Key Point · Representation

Left branch: \(y=x+1\). Right branch: \(y=-x+5\). Open circle at \((2,3)\); filled dot at \((2,1.5)\).

Walk through the solution

Step 1. Left trace: as \(x\to 2^{-}\), outputs on \(y=x+1\) approach 3.

Step 2. Right trace: as \(x\to 2^{+}\), outputs on \(y=-x+5\) approach 3.

Step 3. Compare: \(L^{-}=L^{+}=3\), so the two-sided limit is 3.

Step 4. Filled dot at \((2,1.5)\) gives \(f(2)=1.5\neq 3\) \(\Rightarrow\) not continuous at 2.

From the left
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2^-} f(x) = 3\]
From the right
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2^+} f(x) = 3\]
Two-sided limit
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) = 3\]
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) = 3\]
\[\displaystyle f(2)=1.5\]
AP Checkpoint
Conclusion: Two-sided limit is 3; function value is 1.5 — limit exists but graph is not continuous.
Key Point · Check

Open circle shows approach height 3; filled dot shows \(f(2)=1.5\).

slides.title: Endpoint and one-sided domain
slides.html:
Representation Transfer

When only one side exists

When only one side exists

TransferDomain matters

At an endpoint, a left-hand limit may be undefined.

\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0^+} f(x) = 0\]
Key Point · At x = 0

Only values with \(x\ge 0\) are in the domain, so we trace from the right. There is no left-hand approach on this graph.

slides.title: Worked example: jump discontinuity
slides.html:
Definition · Problem

The left and right branches approach different heights at \(x=3\).

Key Point · Representation

Blue branch from the left; orange branch from the right.

Walk through the solution

Step 1. Left trace: branch height approaches −1.

Step 2. Right trace: branch height approaches 4.

Step 3. Compare: \(-1\neq 4\).

Step 4. Conclusion: the two-sided limit does not exist (jump discontinuity).

From the left
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x) = -1\]
From the right
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x) = 4\]
Two-sided limit
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\ \text{does not exist}\]

The left approach gives -1 but the right gives 4. Because \(L^{-} \neq L^{+}\), the two-sided limit at x = 3 does not exist.

AP Checkpoint
Conclusion: Two-sided limit DNE because one-sided limits disagree.
Key Point · Check

A filled dot at \(f(3)\) would not repair the jump — limits come from branches.

Ready to check?Reveal the model solution only after you've written a full attempt.
From the left
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^-} f(x) = -1\]
From the right
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3^+} f(x) = 4\]
Two-sided limit
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 3} f(x)\ \text{does not exist}\]

The left approach gives -1 but the right gives 4. Because \(L^{-} \neq L^{+}\), the two-sided limit at x = 3 does not exist.

slides.title: Guided: sketch with constraints
slides.html:
Guided ExampleYour turn

Use Thinking Space first; reveal hints only when stuck.

Thinking Space

Write your setup and first step before opening any hint.

Sketch a graph that satisfies all three conditions below.

From the left
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2^-} f(x) = 3\]
From the right
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2^+} f(x) = 3\]
Two-sided limit
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) = 3\]
\[\displaystyle f(2)=-1\]

Branches must approach the open-circle height 3, but the filled dot at \(x=2\) must be at −1.

  • Hint 1: Draw an open circle at \((2,3)\) — this is the approach height.
  • Hint 2: Draw left and right branches that meet that open circle.
  • Hint 3: Place a filled dot at \((2,-1)\) for the function value.
✦
Ready to check?Reveal the model solution only after you've written a full attempt.

Your sketch may differ in shape — check open vs filled points and branch heights.

slides.title: Practice: jump discontinuity
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Unequal one-sided limits → two-sided limit DNE.

At \(x=b\), the left-hand limit is 3 and the right-hand limit is 5. Which statement about the two-sided limit is correct?

From the left
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to b^-} f(x) = 3\]
From the right
\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to b^+} f(x) = 5\]

Choose your answer

C — you cannot average 3 and 5. A jump means the two-sided limit does not exist.

slides.title: Practice: read piecewise graph
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Continuity requires limit = function value.

On the \(x=2\) graph:

\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) = 3\]
\[\displaystyle f(2)=1.5\]

Is \(f\) continuous at \(x=2\)?

Choose your answer

B — the limit exists but does not equal \(f(2)\). Redefining would remove the discontinuity (topic 1.13).

slides.title: Practice: filled dot trap
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Filled dot gives \(f(c)\); limits come from approach along branches.

A student reads \(f(2)=-1\) from a filled dot and concludes the limit at \(x=2\) is \(-1\). What is wrong with that reasoning?

Choose your answer

B — always trace left and right branches first. The filled dot gives \(f(2)\), not the limit.

slides.title: Practice: infinite behavior
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Trace each branch: left goes to \(-\infty\), right goes to \(+\infty\).

Near \(x=0\), the graph of \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}\) shows \(|y|\) growing without bound. Which statement about one-sided and two-sided limits is correct?

\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0} f(x) = ?\]

Choose your answer

B — as \(x\to 0^{-}\), \(y\to -\infty\); as \(x\to 0^{+}\), \(y\to +\infty\). Unequal infinite behavior means the two-sided limit does not exist in \(\mathbb{R}\). C and D describe only one side.

slides.title: Practice: endpoint one-sided limit
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Domain starts at 0; only the right-hand approach exists.

For \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\) on \([0,4]\), which statement is correct at \(x=0\)?

Choose your answer

B — right-hand limit is 0. A is outside the domain. C incorrectly claims a two-sided approach. D — \(f(0)=0\) is defined.

slides.title: Practice: classify discontinuity
slides.html:
Strategy hint

Limit exists but function value is missing — removable hole.

A graph shows the following at \(x=2\):

\[\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 2} f(x) = 3\]
\[\displaystyle f(2)\ \text{is undefined (open circle only)}\]

What type of discontinuity is this?

Choose your answer

B — a hole at \(x=2\). A needs unequal one-sided limits. C involves unbounded behavior. D requires \(f(2)=\) limit.

slides.title: Error analysis: skipping a side
slides.html:
Contrast / Error Analysis

Incomplete traces

Incomplete traces

Common Mistake

Mistake: checking only the left branch because it “looks closer.”

Fix: always record both \(L^{-}\) and \(L^{+}\) in display form before deciding.
